> Two mornings in groups on one of two new datasets. On Friday you present to a
> group that worked on the other one. There is no answer to check against.

## Your group

1. **Find your group** below. Groups A1 to A5 work on Study A, and B1 to B5 on
   Study B.
2. **Split into three pairs** on Wednesday at 10:00. In a group of seven, one
   pair is three people.
3. **Each pair takes one sub-question.** Partners work on the same
   sub-question, but each on their own laptop with their own Pi. You compare at
   the check-ins.

### Find your group

Type part of your name. If your name is missing or spelled wrong, tell one of
the TAs.

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  var input = document.getElementById('group-search');
  var grid = document.getElementById('group-grid');
  var status = document.getElementById('group-search-status');
  var cards = Array.prototype.slice.call(grid.querySelectorAll('.group-card'));
  var norm = function (s) {
    return s.normalize('NFD').replace(/[̀-ͯ]/g, '')
      .replace(/[‘’']/g, '').toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim();
  };
  var items = [];
  cards.forEach(function (card) {
    card.querySelectorAll('li').forEach(function (li) {
      items.push({ card: card, li: li, name: li.textContent, key: norm(li.textContent) });
    });
  });
  var escapeHtml = function (s) {
    return s.replace(/[&<>"]/g, function (c) { return { '&': '&amp;', '<': '&lt;', '>': '&gt;', '"': '&quot;' }[c]; });
  };
  var lastScrolled = null;
  function update() {
    var q = norm(input.value);
    items.forEach(function (it) { it.li.classList.remove('is-match'); it.li.textContent = it.name; });
    cards.forEach(function (c) { c.classList.remove('is-match'); });
    if (q.length < 2) {
      grid.classList.remove('is-searching'); status.textContent = ''; lastScrolled = null; return;
    }
    grid.classList.add('is-searching');
    var words = q.split(' ');
    var hits = items.filter(function (it) {
      return words.every(function (w) { return it.key.indexOf(w) !== -1; });
    });
    cards.forEach(function (c) {
      if (norm(c.dataset.group) === q) { c.classList.add('is-match'); }
    });
    hits.forEach(function (it) {
      it.li.classList.add('is-match');
      it.li.innerHTML = '<mark>' + escapeHtml(it.name) + '</mark>';
      it.card.classList.add('is-match');
    });
    var matched = cards.filter(function (c) { return c.classList.contains('is-match'); });
    if (hits.length === 1) {
      status.textContent = hits[0].name + ': group ' + hits[0].card.dataset.group;
    } else if (hits.length > 1) {
      status.textContent = hits.length + ' names match. Keep typing.';
    } else if (matched.length === 1) {
      status.textContent = 'Group ' + matched[0].dataset.group;
    } else {
      status.textContent = 'No match. Try another part of your name, or ask a TA.';
    }
    if (matched.length === 1 && lastScrolled !== matched[0]) {
      lastScrolled = matched[0];
      matched[0].scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth', block: 'nearest' });
    }
  }
  input.addEventListener('input', update);
})();
</script>
```

## Wednesday

[On your own]{.who .solo} means your own laptop and your own Pi, even though your partner
has the same sub-question. Don't compare notes until the check-in.

| time | who | what |
|---|---|---|
| 9:30 | [Whole group]{.who .group} | Sit together. Open your study's card below the table. |
| 9:40 | [On your own]{.who .solo} | Ask Pi about your dataset. No code yet: what is in each file, how many people are in each arm, what does a column mean? |
| 10:00 | [Whole group]{.who .group} | Pick three sub-questions from your study's card. Split into three pairs and give each pair one sub-question. In each pair, decide who uses which [model](#two-models-in-each-pair). |
| 10:10 | [On your own]{.who .solo} | Write the [QC report](#the-qc-report). |
| 10:30 | [On your own]{.who .solo} | Finish the QC report, then start on your pair's sub-question. |
| 11:00 | | Tea |
| **11:15** | [With your pair]{.who .pair} | [Check-in W1](#check-ins): compare your two QC reports. |
| 11:30 | [On your own]{.who .solo} | Ask Pi for whatever your QC report missed, then carry on with the sub-question. |
| **12:15** | [Whole group]{.who .group} | [Check-in W2](#check-ins): agree one QC decision for the group. |
| 12:35 | [On your own]{.who .solo} | Rerun with the group's QC decision. Before lunch, write a few lines at the top of your `.qmd` saying where you got to. |
| 1:00 | | Lunch |

: {tbl-colwidths="[10,23,67]"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Study A groups (A1 to A5): does a vaginal probiotic change the community?

A randomised trial. Participants received either a live *Lactobacillus crispatus*
product or a placebo, and were sampled before and after the course of treatment.

| | |
|---|---|
| participants | 176 |
| samples | 352, one before and one after per person |
| arms | 121 probiotic, 55 placebo |
| metadata | `arm`, `time_point` (`pre`, `post`), age, pH, Nugent score, Amsel criteria |

: {tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

The arms are unbalanced, 121 against 55, so check your baseline before you
interpret anything about the follow-up.

**Sub-questions.** Pick three, ideally one from each column, so your pairs
cover the bacteria, the host and the link between them.

| Microbiome | Host | Connecting the two |
|---|---|---|
| Did the community shift from pre to post, and differently by arm? *Tuesday's ordination is a good start.* | Did host gene expression change with treatment? *Wednesday afternoon's module covers this; this morning, start by ordinating the genes.* | Did the probiotic only work in people whose community started a certain way? *Tuesday's community grouping is a good start.* |
| Which species changed in the probiotic arm, besides *L. crispatus*? *Wednesday afternoon's module covers this.* | Which biological processes do the gene changes point to? *Harder. Enrichment is taught on Thursday afternoon, so you will learn it from Pi and from reading.* | Do pH, Nugent score and cytokines move with the community change, or on their own? *Tuesday's anatomy module is a good start.* |

: {tbl-colwidths="[33,34,33]"}
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Study B groups (B1 to B5): do hormonal contraceptives differ in their effect?

A cross-sectional comparison of three contraceptive methods, each person sampled
once.

| | |
|---|---|
| participants | 93, one sample each |
| arms | 39 injectable, 28 pill, 26 ring |
| metadata | `arm`, `bv` (Amsel), `nugent`, `ph`, `any_sti` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

Nobody was randomised to a method, and people who choose different methods
differ in other ways. With 93 samples in three groups, ask which of your
comparisons is actually powered.

**Sub-questions.** Pick three, ideally one from each column.

| Microbiome | Host | Connecting the two |
|---|---|---|
| Do the three methods differ in community composition? *Tuesday's ordination is a good start.* | The ring is delivered locally and the other two are systemic. Does the ring differ from the other two in host gene expression? *Wednesday afternoon's module covers this; this morning, start by ordinating the genes.* | Group people by community type, then test their genes. Does community type explain more than the method does? *Tuesday's community grouping is a good start.* |
| Is bacterial vaginosis more common in one arm? *Tuesday's anatomy module is a good start.* | Which biological processes do the ring-versus-systemic genes point to? *Harder. Enrichment is taught on Thursday afternoon, so you will learn it from Pi and from reading.* | Is bacterial vaginosis the explanation for whatever the method seems to do? *Start from your group's other two sub-questions.* |

: {tbl-colwidths="[33,34,33]"}
:::

If your pair finishes early, write your own sub-question and tell the rest of
your group at the next check-in.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Study A groups (A1 to A5): before you finish your slides

- **Baseline.** The arms are 121 against 55. Did the two arms look the same
  before treatment? If not, say so before you show any change.
- **Pre and post.** Each person was sampled twice. Check that your test knows
  the two samples come from the same person.
- **Enrichment.** If your pair took the processes sub-question, say which
  method you used and which source you read for it.
- **Your Friday audience** is B1 to B5. They have not seen this trial, so your
  first slide explains it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Study B groups (B1 to B5): before you finish your slides

- **No randomisation.** People chose their method. Name one way the three arms
  might differ apart from the method.
- **Power.** 93 samples in three arms of 26 to 39. For each comparison you
  show, say how many samples were in it.
- **Ring versus systemic.** If you merged the pill and the injectable, say why
  that is fair.
- **Your Friday audience** is A1 to A5. They have not seen this study, so your
  first slide explains it.
:::

## Friday

| how long | who | what |
|---|---|---|
| 30 minutes | [Whole group]{.who .group} | Run through your deck. Each pair asks another pair one question about their slide. |
| 1 hour | [With your partner group]{.who .group} | A1 sits with B1, A2 with B2, and so on. Present for 30 minutes, then listen to theirs for 30. |

: {tbl-colwidths="[14,26,60]"}

## Two models in each pair

On Wednesday one partner uses `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash`, the default, and the other
switches to `z-ai/glm-5.3` by typing `/model` in Pi. On Thursday you swap. In a
pair of three, two of you use the same model. The stronger model costs roughly
ten times as much for a morning's work, a couple of dollars, which is still a
small part of your budget.

If you are curious on Thursday, try `anthropic/claude-opus-5.5` for a while.
Then look at what it cost on your [OpenRouter activity page](https://openrouter.ai/activity)
and decide for yourself whether it was worth it.

## Your group's deck

Each group gets a shared Google Slides deck on Wednesday morning. From the
start it has a slide for the group's QC decision and one open-questions slide
for each pair. Put anything you and your partner cannot explain yet on your
pair's open-questions slide, and note what you found out as you go, with a link
to whatever you read. On Thursday that slide becomes your "choice we made"
slide.

To get a figure into the deck, ask Pi to save it as a PNG in
`group_project/figures/`, then right-click the file in the Codespace file list
and choose **Download**.

## Sharing a report with your group

A rendered `.html` file keeps its figures and styling in a separate `_files`
folder, so if you download only the `.html` and send it to someone, the
figures are missing. Ask Pi to put everything in one file:

```
Render group_project/01-qc.qmd with embed-resources: true so the HTML
is a single file I can share.
```

Then right-click the `.html` file in the Codespace file list, choose
**Download**, and send it to your group.

If you want every render to do this, ask Pi to add it to the YAML header at the
top of your `.qmd`:

```yaml
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
```

## The QC report

Everyone starts with the same prompt. Copy the one for your study into Pi as it
is.

Study A:

```
Make group_project/01-qc.qmd that checks the quality of the Study A data
before we analyse it. Render it.
```

Study B:

```
Make group_project/01-qc.qmd that checks the quality of the Study B data
before we analyse it. Render it.
```

The prompt is short on purpose. Your partner's model will decide differently
from yours what a quality check needs, and you will compare the two at 11:15.

## Check-ins

::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## W1, Wednesday 11:15, with your partner

1. Open your two QC reports side by side. Does each one check

    - that sample IDs match across all the tables?
    - library sizes in both count tables, and which samples have very few reads?
    - missing metadata?
    - `rnaseq_batch` cross-tabulated against arm (and against time point in Study A)?
    - whether the arms differed at baseline (Study A)?

    For anything missing, ask your Pi to add it.
2. Compare the **Choices made** sections at the end of your two reports. For
   each difference, can either of you say why? If not, add it to your pair's
   open-questions slide.
3. Split the open questions between you.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## W2, Wednesday 12:15, the whole group

1. Each pair shows one figure and its open-questions slide, about three minutes
   per pair.
2. Answer each other's open questions where you can.
3. Agree one QC decision for the whole group: which samples you drop and how you
   filter features. Write it on the QC slide. All three pairs use it from now on.
4. What did your morning cost? Look at your OpenRouter activity page and compare
   the two models.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## T1, Thursday 10:45, with your partner

1. Which approach are you keeping, or are you keeping both to show the result
   does not depend on it? What is your reason, and what did you read that
   supports it?
2. Which one or two figures go in the talk?
3. Turn your open-questions slide into your "choice we made" slide.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## T2, Thursday 11:45, the whole group

1. Write the question for the whole talk in one sentence.
2. Put the slides in order.
3. State the answer as plainly as the data allow.
4. Write down what you do not believe about your own result.
5. Decide who is speaking.
:::

## Deliverables

A presentation that fits your 30-minute slot, containing:

1. the question you settled on, in one sentence
2. what you did, including what you filtered and why
3. two or three figures, each with a caption you read out
4. for each sub-question, a "choice we made" slide: the two routes you and your
   partner were given, which one you kept and why, and one source you opened and
   read yourself, even if Pi found it for you
5. the answer, stated as plainly as the data allow
6. what you do not believe about your own result

The last of these is required. When you are the audience, ask the other group
about theirs. Every analysis this week had something wrong with it, so look for
the problems in yours before you present.

## Advice from the modules

::: {.callout-tip}
## Things that bit people earlier in the week

- Check your sample table and your count matrix are in the same order before you
  run any test.
- Decide your filter before you look at the result, and write down why.
- On a species table, give DESeq2 `poscounts` size factors and check how many
  species they were built from.
- Define a grouping from one table and test the other, never the same table
  twice.
- Look at how lopsided a ranking is before you believe an enrichment.
- Your dataset has an `rnaseq_batch` column. Cross-tabulate it against your
  groups early, and find out whether you have a confound rather than a finding.
:::
